title: Individual, Dictator, and Democratic punishment in public good games with perfect and imperfect observability
abstract: In the context of repeated public good contribution games, we experimentally investigate the impact of democratic punishment, when members of a group decide by majority voting whether to inflict punishment on another member, relative to individual peer-to-peer punishment. Democratic punishment leads to more cooperation and higher average payoffs, both under perfect and imperfect monitoring of contributions, primarily by curbing anti-social punishment and thereby establishing a closer connection between a member's contribution decision and whether subsequently being punished by others. We also find that participating in a democratic punishment procedure makes even non-contributors' punishment intentions more pro-social.
summary_en: When members of a group must vote on whether to punish a transgressor, does democratic punishment work better than peer-to-peer punishment? Ambrus and Greiner experimentally compare democratic punishment (majority vote on whether to punish) with individual peer punishment in repeated public-good games. Democratic punishment leads to more cooperation and higher payoffs under both perfect and imperfect monitoring — primarily by curbing anti-social punishment (punishing high contributors) and creating a clearer link between contribution and being punished. Even non-contributors' punishment intentions become more pro-social when the punishment is collectively decided.
data_used: Lab experiment with public-good contribution games, multiple sessions at university lab venues, comparing democratic, dictatorial, and peer-to-peer punishment treatments under varying monitoring conditions.
policy_relevance: Hungarian local-government and committee-based regulatory bodies (water districts, electricity co-ops, professional associations) often choose between collective and individual sanctioning rules. The paper provides experimental evidence that democratic (collective-vote) sanctioning produces better cooperation outcomes than individual peer-to-peer sanctioning. Useful framework for designing committee-based enforcement at GVH, MNB, and other regulators.
